distractorExplanations.b: Catch-up contributions are employee elective deferrals; employer contributions have no age-50 catch-up amount.
distractorExplanations.c: Catch-up eligibility starts in the year the participant turns 50; 59½ relates to penalty-free distributions.
distractorExplanations.d: Catch-ups may be Roth, and under SECURE 2.0 higher earners' catch-ups must be Roth rather than pre-tax.

prompt: Mortality credits in pooled annuities arise from:

options.text: Insurers guaranteeing payouts with assets held by state guaranty associations
Survivors benefiting from mortality experience of those who die earlier in the pool
Investment returns on the insurer's general account bond portfolio
Annuitants who surrender early forfeiting surrender charges to the pool

explanation: Risk pooling allows higher lifetime payouts than individual investment for some annuitants.

distractorExplanations.a: State guaranty associations back insurer insolvency up to limits; they are not the source of mortality credits.
distractorExplanations.c: General account returns drive the interest component of payouts; mortality credits come from pooling longevity.
distractorExplanations.d: Surrender charges recoup insurer costs on early exits; mortality credits come from those who die, not surrender.

prompt: Health Savings Accounts require the account owner to be enrolled in:

options.text: A high-deductible health plan alongside a general-purpose health FSA
A high-deductible health plan and Medicare Part A as secondary
A high-deductible health plan and have no disqualifying coverage
Any health plan with a deductible of at least $500 per person

explanation: HSA contributions are allowed only when the owner is covered by a high-deductible health plan that meets the IRS deductible and out-of-pocket rules and has no other disqualifying coverage. Enrolling in Medicare, including Part A, ends the right to contribute. A general-purpose health FSA is also disqualifying coverage, and a plan with only a token deductible is not a qualifying high-deductible plan.

distractorExplanations.a: A general-purpose health FSA is disqualifying coverage; limited-purpose FSAs are the HSA-compatible version.
distractorExplanations.b: Any Medicare enrollment, including Part A, ends eligibility to make HSA contributions.
distractorExplanations.d: An HDHP must meet the IRS-indexed minimum deductible (over $1,600 self-only), far above $500.

prompt: Capital needs analysis for life insurance typically starts from:

options.text: A multiple of gross income, such as ten times salary, adjusted for the client's age
The present value of the insured's future earnings net of personal consumption
The lump-sum amount required to fund survivor goals, ignoring existing assets
The lump-sum amount required to fund identified survivor goals, minus existing resources

explanation: Capital needs sizing works backward from specific goals (debt, education, income) rather than from earnings multiples alone. Other survivor income is also netted out.

distractorExplanations.a: Income multiples are a rule of thumb; capital needs analysis builds up from specific survivor goals.
distractorExplanations.b: Discounting future earnings net of consumption is the human life value approach, not capital needs.
distractorExplanations.c: Capital needs analysis subtracts existing assets, insurance, and survivor income; ignoring them overstates coverage.

prompt: Purchasing power risk for retirees means:

options.text: Fixed income may buy fewer goods over time if inflation exceeds income growth
Rising interest rates may cut the market value of existing bond holdings
Withdrawals during early market losses may deplete savings faster
A long lifespan may exhaust savings before the retiree's death

explanation: Purchasing-power risk is the chance that a dollar payment buys less as prices rise. A pension or other income that does not grow with inflation loses real spending power even though the check itself does not shrink. A fall in bond prices when interest rates rise is interest-rate risk, selling assets after early market losses is sequence-of-returns risk, and running out of money over a long life is longevity risk.

distractorExplanations.b: Bond price declines from rising rates are interest-rate risk, not purchasing power risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Early losses combined with withdrawals describe sequence-of-returns risk, not purchasing power risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Outliving savings is longevity risk; purchasing power risk concerns inflation eroding each dollar.

prompt: An adviser who serves as a fiduciary to an employer retirement plan buys fiduciary liability insurance mainly to cover:

options.text: Plan investment losses caused purely by broad market declines
Claims that the adviser breached its ERISA duties to the plan
Theft of plan assets, the risk the required ERISA fidelity bond covers
Negligent planning advice given to individual retail clients

explanation: Fiduciary liability insurance responds to claims that a plan fiduciary breached ERISA duties, such as imprudent fund selection or excessive fees, paying defense costs and damages. Theft is covered by the ERISA fidelity bond, and negligent advice to retail clients falls under professional E&O.

distractorExplanations.a: Neither fiduciary nor E&O policies insure investment performance; market losses on prudent decisions are not a breach claim.
distractorExplanations.c: Theft or fraud by people handling plan assets is covered by the ERISA fidelity bond, not by fiduciary liability insurance.
distractorExplanations.d: Negligent advice to individual retail clients is a professional E&O exposure; fiduciary liability cover targets plan fiduciary breaches.

prompt: A manufacturer promises each retiree a monthly pension equal to 1.5 percent of final average pay times years of service. Assets are pooled, and workers have no individual investment accounts. If investment returns fall short of the funding target, who must make up the shortfall?

options.text: The employer, because the plan promises a formula benefit and the employer bears the investment risk
Each worker, because the monthly pension rises and falls with the return on the pooled assets
The PBGC, because it guarantees the entire promised benefit and applies no monthly cap
The trustee personally, because fiduciary status turns a funding shortfall into the trustee's own debt

explanation: A traditional defined-benefit plan promises a benefit set by a formula, here 1.5 percent of final average pay times service. The employer must fund that promise. If the pooled investments earn less than the funding target, the employer contributes more. Participants do not have separate accounts whose balances determine the pension.

distractorExplanations.b: A benefit that moves with investment results describes a defined-contribution account. This plan promises a formula pension, so workers do not absorb the funding shortfall.
distractorExplanations.c: The PBGC insures most private defined-benefit plans only up to a monthly cap. It does not take over routine investment shortfalls or guarantee an uncapped benefit.
distractorExplanations.d: A trustee must invest prudently, but a funding shortfall remains the employer's contribution obligation. Fiduciary status does not make the trustee personally owe the pension.

prompt: Luis is married and is about to start a defined-benefit pension. He wants a single-life annuity that stops at his death. What payment form must the plan use unless his spouse consents in writing to a different form?

options.text: A qualified joint and survivor annuity that continues an income to his spouse after his death
A lump sum rolled to his IRA, which a married participant may choose without spousal consent
The single-life annuity he requested, which is the automatic form for a married participant
A ten-year period-certain annuity that ends after ten years with no spouse continuation

explanation: ERISA makes a qualified joint and survivor annuity the normal form for a married participant in a defined-benefit pension. That form pays Luis for life and then continues a survivor income to his spouse. The plan can pay a single-life annuity or another form only after his spouse consents in writing to waive the survivor benefit.

distractorExplanations.b: A lump sum is an optional form. Paying it instead of the qualified joint and survivor annuity requires the spouse's written consent; it is not available automatically.
distractorExplanations.c: A single-life annuity ends at Luis's death and leaves the spouse with no continuation. That is the form he wants, but it is not the default while he is married.
distractorExplanations.d: A ten-year period certain is an optional annuity shape. The statutory default for a married pension participant is a qualified joint and survivor annuity.

prompt: Elena's will leaves her probate estate to her son. Her traditional IRA beneficiary form, which she signed after the will, names her sister. Elena dies with her sister and her son both living. Who receives the IRA?

options.text: Her sister, because the IRA beneficiary form controls who receives that account
Her son, because a will signed before the form still directs every retirement account
Her estate, because a difference between the will and the form sends the IRA to probate
Her sister and her son in equal shares, because each document names one family member

explanation: A traditional IRA is a contract with the custodian. The beneficiary form, not the will, names who receives the account. Elena's sister takes the IRA because she is the living person on that form. The will still disposes of probate property, but it does not replace a valid beneficiary designation.

distractorExplanations.b: A will does not override an IRA beneficiary form, whether the will is older or newer. The son inherits probate assets, not the IRA that names the sister.
distractorExplanations.c: A living named beneficiary keeps the IRA out of the probate estate. A difference between the will and the form does not cancel the form.
distractorExplanations.d: The two documents do different jobs. The form gives the IRA to the sister and does not split it with the heir named in the will.

prompt: A homeowner raises the dwelling deductible from $500 to $2,500, and the annual premium falls. In risk-management terms, what tradeoff did the homeowner accept?

options.text: Retaining a larger first layer of each covered loss in exchange for a smaller premium
Transferring more of each loss, because a higher deductible makes the insurer pay sooner
Avoiding dwelling risk, because the higher deductible cancels coverage on the house
Reducing how often a fire occurs, because the deductible changes the chance of a loss

explanation: A deductible is the layer of a covered loss the insured keeps. Moving the deductible from $500 to $2,500 means the homeowner retains an extra $2,000 of each covered dwelling loss, and the insurer begins paying only above the new, higher threshold. The premium falls because less of the small-loss layer is being transferred.

distractorExplanations.b: A higher deductible delays the insurer's payment; the insurer pays less of a small loss, not more. The homeowner kept a larger layer rather than transferring a larger one.
distractorExplanations.c: The dwelling stays insured above $2,500. Raising the deductible changes the retained amount and does not cancel the policy.
distractorExplanations.d: A deductible is a financing choice after a loss. It does not change the probability of a fire or another covered peril.

prompt: A new retiree will draw spending money from Social Security, a small monthly pension, and an investment portfolio. Using all three sources, rather than relying on the portfolio alone, mainly addresses which risk?

options.text: The risk that one income source is cut, delayed, or poorly timed relative to spending
The risk that a higher health-plan deductible will raise this year's insurance premium
Interest-rate risk on a bond ladder that sits inside the pension and nowhere else
The risk that naming both a primary and a contingent beneficiary forces probate

explanation: Retirement-income diversification means the household does not depend on a single paycheck. Social Security, a pension, and portfolio withdrawals can fail or arrive at different times for different reasons. If one source is cut or a market drop makes portfolio sales painful, the other sources still cover part of spending.

distractorExplanations.b: A health-plan deductible is the medical cost the household retains. It has no connection to combining Social Security, a pension, and portfolio withdrawals.
distractorExplanations.c: Interest-rate risk is the sensitivity of bond prices to rate changes. Holding three income sources addresses dependence on any one source, not the duration of pension bonds.
distractorExplanations.d: Primary and contingent beneficiary labels decide who receives an account at death. They are not the reason for drawing retirement spending from three sources.

prompt: A 401(k) participant asks the plan to mail an eligible rollover check payable to her, and she plans to deposit it in an IRA within 60 days. The plan must withhold 20 percent. Which statement is correct?

options.text: She must add the withheld 20 percent from other funds if the entire distribution is to be rolled over
The 20 percent withholding is an extra penalty that cannot be credited against her income tax
A trustee-to-trustee direct rollover of the same dollars is also subject to the 20 percent withholding
The 60-day clock starts after she sends the withheld 20 percent back to the plan

explanation: When a qualified plan pays an eligible rollover distribution to the participant, it withholds 20 percent. That amount is income-tax withholding, not a separate penalty, and it is credited on her return. If she wants the full distribution treated as rolled over, she must make up the withheld 20 percent from other savings. A direct trustee-to-trustee rollover is not paid to her and is not subject to that withholding. The 60 days run from the day she receives the distribution.

distractorExplanations.b: The 20 percent is federal income-tax withholding and is credited against tax on the return. It is not an extra penalty stacked on top of ordinary income.
distractorExplanations.c: A direct trustee-to-trustee rollover is not paid to the participant, so the mandatory 20 percent withholding on a check payable to her does not apply to it.
distractorExplanations.d: The 60 days start when she receives the distribution. She does not restart that clock by sending money back to the plan; the makeup amount goes into the IRA.

prompt: A disability income policy pays no monthly benefit during the first 90 days of a covered disability. In risk-management terms, what is that 90-day elimination period?

options.text: A time deductible: the insured retains the income lost during those first 90 days
A coinsurance clause: the insurer pays 90 percent of lost income starting on day one
A waiver of premium: premiums stop once a disability has lasted 90 days
An inflation rider: the benefit increases by 90 percent when the waiting period ends

explanation: The elimination period is the stretch of disability the insured must absorb before benefits begin. Like a dollar deductible, it is retained risk. The insured keeps the lost income for those 90 days, and the insurer starts the monthly benefit only after that waiting period ends.

distractorExplanations.b: Coinsurance splits each dollar of a covered loss by a percentage. A 90-day elimination period delays the start of benefits; it does not pay 90 percent from the first day.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiver of premium stops premium charges while the insured is disabled. It is a separate policy feature, not the waiting period before income benefits begin.
distractorExplanations.d: An inflation rider changes the monthly benefit over time. The elimination period does not raise the benefit by 90 percent.

prompt: Which of the following actions transfers a pure risk, rather than retaining it, avoiding it, or reducing its severity?

options.text: Paying a premium so an insurer bears the financial loss if the insured dies during the term
Holding cash equal to a deductible and buying no coverage for that first layer of loss
Choosing not to buy a rental house so a tenant-injury claim cannot arise
Installing a sprinkler system that limits how severe a fire loss would be

explanation: Risk transfer shifts the financial consequence of a loss to another party, usually an insurer, in exchange for a premium. Term life insurance transfers the financial risk of dying during the term, which is a pure risk because it involves a chance of loss and no chance of gain. Cash for a deductible retains risk, declining the rental avoids the exposure, and a sprinkler system reduces severity.

distractorExplanations.b: Funding a deductible with cash is retention. The household keeps that layer of loss instead of paying an insurer to take it.
distractorExplanations.c: Not buying the rental removes the exposure entirely. That is risk avoidance, not a transfer of an existing risk to an insurer.
distractorExplanations.d: A sprinkler system is loss control. It reduces how bad a fire would be, while the owner still bears the remaining loss unless insurance is also bought.

prompt: Nora names her spouse as primary beneficiary of her IRA and her brother as contingent beneficiary. Nora dies while her spouse is still living and has not disclaimed the account. Who receives the IRA?

options.text: Her brother, because a contingent beneficiary shares the account with the primary beneficiary
Her spouse, because a contingent beneficiary is paid only if the primary beneficiary does not take
Her estate, because naming both a primary and a contingent beneficiary cancels the form
Her spouse and her brother in equal shares, because both names appear on the form

explanation: The primary beneficiary receives the IRA if that person survives the owner and accepts the account. A contingent beneficiary is a backup. Nora's spouse is alive and has not disclaimed, so the spouse takes the IRA. Her brother would be considered only if the spouse were already dead or declined the account.

distractorExplanations.a: A contingent beneficiary does not share with the primary. The brother is skipped while the spouse survives and accepts the IRA.
distractorExplanations.c: Naming a primary and a contingent is the ordinary way to complete the form. Those two labels do not void the designation or send the IRA to the estate.
distractorExplanations.d: The form does not split the IRA between the primary and the contingent. The contingent receives nothing when the primary takes the account.

prompt: A plan statement shows each worker a hypothetical account that grows with pay credits and a stated interest credit. Workers do not direct the investments, and the sponsor must fund the promised credits. How should a planner classify this plan?

options.text: A defined-contribution plan, because each worker owns the account and bears the investment risk
A defined-benefit plan, because the sponsor promises the credits and bears the investment risk
An unfunded nonqualified plan, because pay credits are a bookkeeping promise outside ERISA
A Roth account, because the interest credit is tax-free and the sponsor gets no deduction

explanation: A cash-balance plan is a defined-benefit plan that states the promise as a hypothetical account. Pay credits and interest credits are bookkeeping entries, not a separate account the worker invests. The sponsor funds the plan and bears the risk that actual investment results differ from the crediting rate. The benefit is a qualified pension promise, not a Roth balance and not an unfunded executive promise.

distractorExplanations.a: The account is hypothetical. Calling the plan defined contribution confuses the statement format with who bears the investment risk, which remains with the sponsor.
distractorExplanations.c: Cash-balance plans are qualified defined-benefit plans. The credits are not an unfunded nonqualified promise sitting outside ERISA.
distractorExplanations.d: An interest credit is part of a pre-tax benefit formula. It is not Roth earnings, and the sponsor's contributions are deductible under qualified-plan rules.

prompt: A retiree uses part of her portfolio to buy a single-life immediate annuity that pays the same dollar amount each month for as long as she lives. Which risk did that purchase transfer to the insurer?

options.text: Inflation risk, because a fixed annuity payment rises with the cost of living each year
Longevity risk, because the insurer must keep paying if she lives far longer than average
Sequence risk on the assets she kept, because the annuity reinsures market losses in that portfolio
Sponsor insolvency of her old pension, because the annuity guarantees that separate employer plan

explanation: A life annuity transfers longevity risk. The insurer pools many lives and must continue this retiree's payment no matter how long she lives, funding part of that promise with mortality experience. A fixed dollar payment does not move inflation risk to the insurer. The annuity also does not insure market losses on assets she did not annuitize, and it is not a guarantee of a different employer's pension.

distractorExplanations.a: A fixed annuity stays at the same dollar amount. Inflation protection would require a rising payment or a cost-of-living feature, which this contract does not have.
distractorExplanations.c: Sequence risk on the portfolio she kept is still hers. The insurer took longevity risk only on the premium she paid in.
distractorExplanations.d: The annuity is a contract with the issuing insurer. It does not guarantee a former employer's pension if that sponsor fails.

prompt: A covered health bill is $10,000. The policy has a $1,000 deductible and then 20 percent coinsurance, and no out-of-pocket maximum has been reached. How much does the insured pay on this bill?

options.text: $1,800, the 20 percent coinsurance on the $9,000 above the deductible, with the deductible left out
$2,800, the $1,000 deductible plus 20 percent of the $9,000 that remains above the deductible
$7,200, the insurer's 80 percent share of the $9,000 above the deductible
$9,000, the portion of the bill left after subtracting the deductible

explanation: The insured pays the $1,000 deductible first. Coinsurance applies to the remaining $9,000, and 20 percent of $9,000 is $1,800. The insured's total is $1,000 plus $1,800, or $2,800. The insurer pays the other $7,200. Stopping at the coinsurance piece, or reporting the insurer's share, answers a different question.

distractorExplanations.a: $1,800 is only the 20 percent coinsurance on the $9,000 above the deductible. The insured also pays the $1,000 deductible, so the bill is not limited to the coinsurance piece.
distractorExplanations.c: $7,200 is what the insurer pays after the deductible and 20 percent coinsurance. The question asks for the insured's cost, which is the other $2,800.
distractorExplanations.d: $9,000 is the amount coinsurance applies to, not the amount the insured pays. The insured pays $1,000 plus 20 percent of that $9,000.

prompt: Why is naming the estate as beneficiary of a traditional IRA usually a weaker choice than naming a person on the beneficiary form?

options.text: The estate label lets a surviving spouse roll the IRA into the spouse's own IRA with no further steps
The account generally goes through probate, and the people who inherit lose the options a named beneficiary would have
The custodian must convert the IRA to a Roth IRA in the year of death
Distributions stop, because an estate is not a person and does not have to withdraw the balance

explanation: An IRA payable to the estate is collected by the estate and administered in probate under the will or intestacy. The people who ultimately receive the money do not get the cleaner choices a person named on the form would have, including a surviving spouse's ability to treat the IRA as the spouse's own. Naming a person on the form keeps that contract path open.

distractorExplanations.a: A spousal rollover is available when the spouse is named on the beneficiary form. Routing the IRA through the estate blocks that direct spousal treatment.
distractorExplanations.c: Death does not force a Roth conversion. A conversion is a separate taxable choice and is not a result of naming the estate.
distractorExplanations.d: The balance still has to be paid out. Naming the estate does not freeze distributions or treat the estate as exempt from withdrawal rules.

prompt: A business owner wants a qualified trust plan, not a set of IRAs. She wants to vary the employer contribution from year to year, including a year with no contribution, and each participant will bear the investment results of an individual account. Which plan fits?

options.text: A money-purchase pension, which requires the same percentage of pay to be contributed every year
A profit-sharing plan, with discretionary employer contributions and participant-directed account risk
A defined-benefit pension that promises a monthly benefit and leaves investment risk with the employer
A salary-deferral arrangement in which the employer is barred from adding any contribution

explanation: A profit-sharing plan is a defined-contribution plan held in a qualified trust. The employer decides the contribution each year and may contribute nothing in a lean year, subject to the plan remaining a real, ongoing plan. Each participant has an account and bears its investment results. There is no promised monthly pension, and the plan is not an IRA arrangement.

distractorExplanations.a: A money-purchase pension requires the formula contribution every year. That fixed annual obligation is the opposite of a contribution the owner may skip.
distractorExplanations.c: A formula monthly pension, with the employer bearing investment risk, is a defined-benefit plan. This owner wants individual accounts and discretionary contributions.
distractorExplanations.d: The defining profit-sharing contribution comes from the employer. Employee deferrals can be added through a 401(k) feature, but the employer is not barred from contributing.

prompt: A planner covers a couple's essential bills with Social Security, a pension, and a fixed life annuity, then leaves the portfolio for travel and other wants. What is the main point of building that income floor?

options.text: To remove inflation risk, because Social Security, pensions, and fixed annuities all rise with prices
To pay must-cover bills from contractual income so a market drop does not force the sale of the whole lifestyle
To skip beneficiary designations, because contractual income does not need a survivor or beneficiary named
To replace health coverage, because the floor pays medical deductibles and coinsurance

explanation: An income floor assigns contractual sources to essential spending and leaves the portfolio for discretionary spending. After a market drop, the couple can cut travel rather than sell assets to buy groceries. That is diversification of retirement income by job. It does not mean every source rises with prices, and it does not replace health insurance or beneficiary planning.

distractorExplanations.a: Social Security has a cost-of-living adjustment, but a fixed pension or a fixed annuity does not automatically rise with prices. The floor does not erase inflation risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Pensions and annuities still use survivor elections, and retirement accounts still need beneficiaries. The floor does not retire those designations.
distractorExplanations.d: The floor is cash for living costs. Medical deductibles and coinsurance are handled by health insurance, Medicare, and any supplement, not by the income floor.

prompt: An IRA owner names her two children, per stirpes, as beneficiaries. One child dies before her, leaving two grandchildren. The other child is alive when the owner dies. How is the IRA divided?

options.text: The living child receives the entire IRA, and the predeceased child's branch is dropped
The living child and the two grandchildren each receive one-third of the IRA
The living child receives half, and the two grandchildren share the predeceased child's half
The estate receives the predeceased child's half, and the living child receives the other half

explanation: Per stirpes divides the account by branch. Each of the two children is a branch, so each branch is entitled to half. The living child takes that child's half. The predeceased child's half stays in that branch and is split between that child's two children. The share does not move to the estate, and the living child does not absorb the whole IRA.

distractorExplanations.a: Giving everything to the living child drops the predeceased child's line. That is not per stirpes; per stirpes keeps that child's share for his or her descendants.
distractorExplanations.b: One-third each would split the IRA equally among all living descendants. Per stirpes gives equal shares to the two branches, not equal shares to each living person.
distractorExplanations.d: Per stirpes sends the predeceased child's share down that child's line. It does not redirect that half to the probate estate.

prompt: A bakery owner wants to deposit employer contributions into a traditional IRA for herself and each eligible employee. She wants the freedom to contribute in some years and not in others, and she does not want a trusteed pension plan. Which arrangement fits?

options.text: A defined-benefit pension that promises a formula benefit and is covered by PBGC insurance
An employee-deferral plan in which the employer is not allowed to make a contribution
A SEP IRA, funded by employer contributions into a traditional IRA for each eligible employee
A Roth IRA program, so retirement withdrawals are tax-free no matter how new the account is

explanation: A SEP IRA is an employer-funded defined-contribution arrangement. The employer contributes, on a basis that can vary by year, into a traditional IRA for each eligible employee. It is not a promised pension and it does not use a trusteed defined-benefit plan. The contributions are pre-tax traditional IRA contributions, not Roth contributions, and employees are not the ones making the SEP contribution.

distractorExplanations.a: A SEP does not promise a formula pension and is not a PBGC-insured defined-benefit plan. The worker simply has an IRA balance funded by the employer.
distractorExplanations.b: Employee salary deferrals, with no employer money, describe a different kind of plan. In a SEP the employer makes the contribution.
distractorExplanations.d: SEP contributions go into traditional IRAs and are pre-tax. Roth treatment, and the holding-period rule for qualified Roth withdrawals, does not describe the SEP contribution.

prompt: An executive's nonqualified deferred-compensation plan is an unfunded promise to pay her later from the company's general assets. Which risk does she accept that a participant in the company's 401(k) does not accept in the same way?

options.text: Market risk on a diversified fund menu held in a trust for the participant's benefit
The risk that her salary deferrals exceed the qualified-plan catch-up rules
The company's credit risk, because general creditors can reach the deferred pay if the company fails
Required minimum distributions on the same schedule that applies to her traditional IRA

explanation: An unfunded nonqualified deferred-compensation promise uses the employer's general assets. If the company fails, its creditors can reach those assets, so the executive bears the company's credit risk. A 401(k) balance is held in a trust for participants and is not an asset the employer's creditors take in the same way. The deferred-compensation contract is also governed by its own terms, not by the IRA required-minimum-distribution schedule.

distractorExplanations.a: Market risk on a fund menu inside a trust describes the 401(k). An unfunded promise is not a participant-directed account held for her benefit.
distractorExplanations.b: Qualified-plan catch-up limits apply to deferrals inside plans such as a 401(k). They are not the distinctive risk of an unfunded company promise.
distractorExplanations.d: IRA required minimum distributions follow the IRA rules. An unfunded deferred-compensation plan follows its contract and the nonqualified-plan distribution rules, not the IRA calendar.

prompt: A person applies for life insurance on a neighbor. She has no family, business, or creditor relationship with the neighbor, and she names herself as beneficiary. Why should the insurer refuse to issue the policy?

options.text: The application names no deductible, and every life policy must include a dollar deductible
Life insurance transfers speculative investment risk, which an insurer is not permitted to accept
She has no insurable interest in the neighbor's life, so the contract would be a wager on a stranger
The death benefit must be payable to the insured's estate, and a living person cannot be beneficiary

explanation: Life insurance requires an insurable interest, such as a close family tie, a business relationship, or a real creditor exposure, so the buyer is covering a genuine loss. A neighbor with none of those ties gives the applicant no insurable interest. Issuing the policy would let her wager on a stranger's death, and the insurer should refuse it.

distractorExplanations.a: Term and permanent life insurance do not use a property-style deductible. The defect in this application is the missing insurable interest, not a blank deductible.
distractorExplanations.b: Dying during the term is a pure risk, a chance of loss without a chance of gain. Speculative risk, such as owning stock, is not what a life policy transfers.
distractorExplanations.d: Once an insurable interest exists, the owner may name a person as beneficiary. The estate is not the required payee, and that is not why this application fails.

prompt: Marcus is married and wants his sister to be the sole beneficiary of his ERISA 401(k). What must happen before the plan can honor that designation?

options.text: He must revise his will, because the will controls 401(k) beneficiaries for a married participant
His sister must sign the form, because a non-spouse beneficiary has to accept the naming in writing
His spouse must consent in writing, because ERISA protects the spouse's right to the death benefit
The balance must be converted to a Roth 401(k), because a sibling can be named on Roth money

explanation: ERISA protects a surviving spouse's right to the qualified-plan death benefit. A married participant may name someone else only if the spouse consents in writing in the manner the plan requires. Changing the will, collecting the sister's signature, or converting to Roth does not replace that spousal consent.

distractorExplanations.a: A will does not override the plan beneficiary rules. For a married participant, the spouse's written consent is what allows a non-spouse to be named.
distractorExplanations.b: The person who must consent is the spouse whose protected right is being given up. The sister's signature does not waive the spouse's right.
distractorExplanations.d: Roth or pre-tax treatment does not change the beneficiary rule. A sibling can be named on either type of account only after the spouse consents.

prompt: Priya's auto policy has a $1,000 collision deductible. She has a covered collision loss of $6,000 and no other insurance on that loss. How much does the insurer pay?

options.text: $1,000, the deductible Priya retains, reported as if it were the insurer's payment
$4,000, the result of subtracting the $1,000 deductible from the $6,000 loss twice
$5,000, the $6,000 covered loss minus the $1,000 deductible she retains
$6,000, the entire loss, as though the deductible were not applied

explanation: On a covered collision, the deductible is the amount the insured retains. Priya keeps the first $1,000 of the $6,000 loss, and the insurer pays the remaining $5,000. The insurer does not pay the deductible itself, does not pay the whole loss, and does not subtract the deductible a second time.

distractorExplanations.a: $1,000 is the layer Priya retains. The insurer pays the loss above that deductible, so its payment is not the deductible amount.
distractorExplanations.b: Subtracting the $1,000 deductible twice produces $4,000 and double-counts the retained layer. The deductible comes off the $6,000 loss once.
distractorExplanations.d: Paying the full $6,000 would ignore the deductible. The contract leaves the first $1,000 with Priya and pays the other $5,000.

prompt: A public-school teacher elects to defer part of her salary into an individual-account plan the district offers. The plan works like a private-sector 401(k) and is the arrangement used by public schools and many tax-exempt employers. Which plan type is it?

options.text: A defined-benefit pension that promises a formula annuity and places investment risk on the district
A SEP IRA funded by employer deposits alone, with no salary-deferral feature for the teacher
A 403(b) plan, the salary-deferral arrangement used by public schools and many nonprofits
An unfunded deferred-compensation promise that remains exposed to the district's creditors

explanation: A 403(b) plan is the salary-reduction retirement plan for public-school employees and employees of many tax-exempt organizations. Like a 401(k), the teacher elects to defer pay into an individual account and bears the investment risk of that account. It is not the district's formula pension, not an employer-only SEP, and not an unfunded promise to pay from the district's general assets.

distractorExplanations.a: A formula annuity, with the employer bearing investment risk, is a defined-benefit pension. A 403(b) is an individual account funded by deferrals and any employer contributions.
distractorExplanations.b: A SEP is an employer-funded IRA arrangement and is not the salary-reduction plan a public school offers in the role of a 401(k).
distractorExplanations.d: A 403(b) account is held for the employee. It is not an unfunded deferred-compensation promise that the district's creditors can reach.

prompt: Ken's pension covers his essential bills, and he uses his portfolio only for travel. Compared with paying every expense from the portfolio, how does the pension change his exposure to sequence-of-returns risk?

options.text: It removes sequence risk, because a pension guarantees that the portfolio itself cannot fall in a down market
It increases sequence risk, because a pension requires larger portfolio withdrawals in the early retirement years
It lowers the withdrawals he must take from the portfolio, so early market losses do less damage to his spending
It renames sequence risk as inflation risk, because a pension has no effect on withdrawals and returns

explanation: Sequence-of-returns risk is most damaging when the retiree must sell assets after early losses. A pension that pays essential bills lets Ken withdraw less from the portfolio in a bad market, or skip a withdrawal for those bills. The portfolio can still decline, but the spending plan depends less on selling into that decline.

distractorExplanations.a: The pension does not freeze the portfolio's market value. It reduces how much he must withdraw, which is a smaller exposure, not immunity from market declines.
distractorExplanations.b: A pension that covers essential bills lowers the amount he needs from the portfolio. It does not force larger withdrawals in the early years.
distractorExplanations.d: Inflation risk is lost purchasing power. The pension's effect here is fewer forced sales, which is a direct change in sequence exposure, not a new name for inflation.

prompt: Helen dies owning a life insurance policy. The named beneficiary, her adult daughter, receives the death benefit in a lump sum. How is that benefit generally treated on the daughter's federal income-tax return?

options.text: It is fully taxable as ordinary income in the year received, like a distribution from a pre-tax retirement account
It is taxed as a long-term capital gain because the policy was a capital asset held for investment
It is tax-free when the beneficiary is a surviving spouse, so a child must include the benefit in income
It is generally excluded from her gross income because it is a life insurance benefit paid by reason of death

explanation: A life insurance death benefit paid to a named beneficiary by reason of the insured's death is generally excluded from the beneficiary's gross income. The daughter does not report the lump sum as ordinary income or as capital gain. The exclusion does not depend on the beneficiary being a spouse. Interest paid later for a delayed settlement is a separate amount and is not the death benefit itself.

distractorExplanations.a: Ordinary-income treatment fits a distribution from a pre-tax retirement account. A life insurance death benefit paid by reason of death is generally excluded from income.
distractorExplanations.b: The death benefit is not treated as the sale of a capital asset. The exclusion comes from the life-insurance rule for amounts paid by reason of death, not from a holding period.
distractorExplanations.c: The income-tax exclusion does not require the beneficiary to be a spouse. A child named on the policy also generally receives the death benefit free of income tax.

prompt: A small employer with no other retirement plan wants a plan that uses IRAs, lets employees defer salary, and requires the employer to contribute every year, either as a match or as a nonelective amount. Which plan type is that?

options.text: A defined-benefit plan that promises a pension based on final average pay
A profit-sharing plan whose employer contribution is discretionary and may be zero in a given year
An employer-funded IRA arrangement in which employees are not permitted to defer salary
A SIMPLE IRA, combining employee salary deferrals with a required employer match or nonelective contribution

explanation: A SIMPLE IRA is a simplified plan for smaller employers that uses IRAs. Employees elect how much salary to defer, and the employer must contribute each year, either by matching deferrals or by making a nonelective contribution for eligible employees. It is not a final-average-pay pension, and the employer cannot treat the contribution as optional the way a profit-sharing contribution is optional.

distractorExplanations.a: A pension based on final average pay is a defined-benefit formula. A SIMPLE IRA is an individual account funded with deferrals and a required employer contribution.
distractorExplanations.b: A profit-sharing employer contribution can be zero in a year. A SIMPLE IRA requires the employer contribution the plan elected, either the match or the nonelective amount.
distractorExplanations.c: An arrangement funded only by the employer, with no employee deferrals, describes a SEP. Employee deferrals are a core feature of a SIMPLE IRA.

prompt: A planner tells a client to insure losses that would wreck the household and to keep small, predictable losses through a higher deductible and a cash reserve. Which risk-management principle is that?

options.text: Insurable interest, which requires the client to buy a policy on each neighbor's life
Adverse selection, which assigns small losses to the insurer and catastrophic losses to the client
Moral hazard, which says a higher deductible gives the client a reason to cause a larger loss
The large-loss principle: spend premium dollars on severity the household cannot absorb, and retain the small layer

explanation: The large-loss principle says limited premium dollars should transfer the losses that would do serious financial harm, while small losses are cheaper to retain. A higher deductible and a cash reserve leave the frequent, affordable layer with the client and leave the catastrophic layer with the insurer. That is a choice about which severity to transfer, not a rule about insurable interest or about who tends to buy insurance.

distractorExplanations.a: Insurable interest is the requirement of a real economic loss before a policy is issued. It does not say to insure catastrophes and retain small losses, and it does not require policies on neighbors.
distractorExplanations.b: This choice reverses the principle. Adverse selection is the tendency of higher-risk people to buy more coverage, not a rule that the insurer should keep small losses.
distractorExplanations.c: Moral hazard is a greater temptation to be careless when someone else pays. A higher deductible reduces that temptation by leaving small losses with the client.

prompt: After a divorce, Jordan rewrites his will to leave everything to his children. He never changes the beneficiary form on his ERISA 401(k), which still names his former spouse, and no QDRO assigns the account. If Jordan dies, who takes the 401(k)?

options.text: The children, because a will signed after the divorce replaces any beneficiary form that names a former spouse
The estate, because a divorce voids beneficiary forms on qualified plans and the account falls into probate
The children and the former spouse in equal shares, because the will and the beneficiary form are both valid
The former spouse, because the plan pays the beneficiary on file and the new will does not replace that form

explanation: An ERISA plan pays the beneficiary designated under the plan's terms. Jordan's form still names his former spouse, and nothing in the facts says the plan accepted a new form or that a QDRO redirected the account. A later will disposes of probate property. It does not rewrite the 401(k) beneficiary, and a state rule that revokes gifts to a former spouse does not override the federal plan document.

distractorExplanations.a: A will changes gifts inside the will. It does not replace an ERISA beneficiary form, and a post-divorce will does not by itself remove a former spouse whom the form still names.
distractorExplanations.b: Divorce does not automatically clear the beneficiary form or send the 401(k) to probate. The plan follows the form on file unless it is changed or a QDRO orders otherwise.
distractorExplanations.c: The plan does not split the account between the will's heirs and the named beneficiary. The form on file controls the 401(k) balance.

prompt: A defined-benefit participant can take a life annuity or a lump sum, which she would roll into an IRA and invest herself. Choosing the lump sum, rather than the life annuity, does which of the following?

options.text: Transfers longevity risk on the full IRA balance to the PBGC
Leaves investment risk with the employer, because the IRA remains inside the pension plan
Removes inflation risk, because an IRA withdrawal can be set once and will keep its purchasing power
Moves longevity risk and investment risk from the pension plan back to the participant

explanation: The life annuity leaves longevity risk, and the plan's investment program, with the pension. Taking the lump sum cashes out that promise. After the money is rolled to her IRA, she bears the market results and the chance of outliving the balance. PBGC protection applies to benefits that stay inside a covered defined-benefit plan, not to an IRA, and a self-managed withdrawal does not lock in purchasing power.

distractorExplanations.a: PBGC insurance applies to benefits inside a covered defined-benefit plan, up to its cap. A lump sum rolled to an IRA is no longer a PBGC-insured pension benefit.
distractorExplanations.b: Once the lump sum is paid and rolled to an IRA, the employer is no longer funding or investing that money. The participant bears the IRA's investment results.
distractorExplanations.c: An IRA withdrawal does not hold its purchasing power by itself. If prices rise, a fixed dollar withdrawal buys less, so the lump sum does not remove inflation risk.

prompt: A pension pays a joint and 50 percent survivor annuity. While both spouses are alive the benefit is $2,000 a month. The participant then dies. How much will the surviving spouse receive over the following 12 months?

options.text: $0, because a joint annuity stops when the participant dies
$2,000, equal to one month of the benefit paid while both spouses were alive
$6,000, the result of cutting the $2,000 benefit in half twice and then multiplying by 12
$12,000, equal to 50 percent of the $2,000 monthly benefit paid for each of 12 months

explanation: Under a joint and 50 percent survivor annuity, the surviving spouse continues to receive 50 percent of the joint benefit. Fifty percent of $2,000 is $1,000 a month. Over the 12 months in the question, that is 12 times $1,000, or $12,000. The income does not stop at the participant's death, and it does not continue at the full $2,000 unless a 100 percent survivor option was elected.

distractorExplanations.a: $0 is the survivor result of a single-life annuity, which ends at the participant's death. The joint and survivor form exists so the spouse keeps receiving a benefit.
distractorExplanations.b: $2,000 is a single monthly joint payment, not twelve months of the survivor benefit. The survivor percentage still has to be applied, and then the months have to be counted.
distractorExplanations.c: $6,000 applies the 50 percent cut a second time, turning $1,000 a month into $500. The election cuts the $2,000 joint benefit once, to $1,000 a month.

prompt: A client holds most of her retirement savings in her employer's stock inside the 401(k), and her paycheck from that same employer is her other major resource. Why is that a weak retirement-income design?

options.text: Employer stock inside a 401(k) is a prohibited investment, so the plan must sell it immediately
A concentrated employer-stock position removes inflation risk, while a diversified fund would add it
The concentration matters for the beneficiary form and has no effect on her income while she is alive
Her paycheck and her savings both depend on one firm, so a business failure can cut her job and her portfolio together

explanation: Diversifying retirement income means the paycheck and the portfolio should not collapse for the same reason. Employer stock ties her financial capital to the same company that pays her wages, which is her human capital. If that firm fails, she can lose her job and a large part of her retirement savings at the same time. Spreading the portfolio across other assets separates those two risks.

distractorExplanations.a: Employer stock is not automatically a prohibited 401(k) investment. The planning problem is the correlated exposure to one firm, not an automatic duty to sell at once.
distractorExplanations.b: A single stock does not remove inflation risk. Diversification spreads sources of return and income; it is not a device that adds inflation.
distractorExplanations.c: The harm shows up during her working life and in retirement: job loss and portfolio loss can arrive together. Beneficiary wording is a separate estate-planning choice.
